nameStory: The Acadian hermit crab gets its name from Acadia, the historical region covering parts of the Maritime Provinces and northern New England where French colonists first settled. This little crab was likely first studied and described from specimens found in these cold Atlantic waters. Like all hermit crabs, it earned the 'hermit' part of its name from its solitary lifestyle, carrying its borrowed shell home wherever it goes.
description: The Acadian hermit crab is a small marine crustacean that lives inside empty snail shells for protection, since its soft, curved abdomen lacks the hard shell that covers most crabs. Unlike true crabs, hermit crabs have asymmetrical bodies perfectly shaped to coil inside spiral shells. They're typically rusty orange to reddish-brown in color with darker banded legs. These crabs are common in New England's cold Atlantic waters, usually measuring about an inch across when fully grown.

idTips.label: Shell-dwelling behavior
idTips.description: Always found living inside an empty snail shell, with only its claws, legs, and front body visible - the soft, curved abdomen stays hidden inside

idTips.label: Claw size difference
idTips.description: Right claw is noticeably larger than the left and feels quite solid when gently touched - used like a door to seal the shell opening when threatened

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Body and legs are typically rusty orange to reddish-brown with darker bands, feeling smooth but slightly bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Walking pattern
idTips.description: Moves in a distinctive dragging motion, pulling its heavy shell home along - you can hear the shell scraping against rocks

idTips.label: Eye stalks
idTips.description: Two prominent, mobile eye stalks that can retract quickly when approached - they feel firm but flexible if gently touched

idTips.label: Cold water preference
idTips.description: Most active in the chilly waters of Maine and northern New England - rarely found in warmer southern waters

habitat: Look for Acadian hermit crabs in rocky tide pools, under seaweed, and on sandy or muddy bottoms in cold Atlantic waters from the intertidal zone down to about 100 feet deep. They're most common along Maine's rocky coastline and in areas with plenty of empty periwinkle and moon snail shells to inhabit. You'll often find them scuttling around tide pools at low tide, especially in areas with lots of algae and small invertebrates to eat.

seasonality.spring: Hermit crabs become more active as waters warm slightly, moving into shallower areas. This is prime time for tide pool exploring as they venture closer to shore.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with peak feeding and shell-switching behavior. Best season for observation as they're commonly found in accessible tide pools during low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Look for them under rockweed and in deeper tide pools as temperatures start dropping.
seasonality.winter: Less active and found in deeper water or well-protected areas. Rarely seen in shallow tide pools, but may be found under rocks in the lowest tidal zones.

funFact: When an Acadian hermit crab outgrows its shell, it will actually line up with other hermit crabs to form a 'vacancy chain' - they'll literally queue up in size order and rapidly swap shells like a perfectly choreographed musical chairs, with each crab moving into the larger shell vacated by the crab ahead of it!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Long-claw Hermit Crab, but Acadians prefer colder water and have more orange-red coloring compared to the Long-claw's more muted brown tones. Memory trick: 'Acadian = Atlantic cold = orange-red' versus Long-claw's longer claws and preference for slightly warmer waters further south.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be fooled by the name 'hermit' - while they live alone in their shells, these crabs are actually quite social and will gather in groups, especially when prime real estate (empty shells) is available. The term 'hermit' refers more to their solitary shell-dwelling lifestyle rather than being antisocial.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Long-claw Hermit Crab, the Acadian hermit has a more robust build and prefers colder waters further north. The Flat-clawed Hermit Crab has distinctly flattened claws and tends to use larger shells, while the Acadian typically inhabits smaller periwinkle or moon snail shells. Acadian hermits also show more vivid orange-red coloration than most of their relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hermit crabs, the Long-claw is distinguished by its notably slender, elongated claws compared to the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab's broad, flattened pincers.

Among New England's hermit crabs, the flat-clawed hermit is unmistakable due to its shield-like claws - the long-claw hermit has thin, extended claws, while the Acadian hermit has more typical rounded pincers.
Among New England's hermit crabs, the hairy hermit is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, bristled legs - its relatives like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed hermit crabs have smooth legs and claws.

Unlike its relatives the Long-claw Hermit (which has elongated claws) and Flat-clawed Hermit (which has flattened, broad claws), the Brown Banded Hermit has proportionally normal-sized claws but sports those unmistakable brown leg bands.
